question.text: Under the eligibility criteria for the Reverse Mortgage Scheme, what is the minimum residual life of the residential property required?

explanation.text: The Logic: One of the core eligibility conditions for the Reverse Mortgage Scheme is that the residual life of the residential property used as collateral must be at least 20 years. The lender needs reasonable assurance that the property will retain economic value over the long disbursement period (and beyond the borrower's life expectancy), so a sufficiently long remaining useful life is required alongside other conditions such as the borrower's age, clear ownership title, absence of encumbrance, and use of the property as the borrower's primary residence. The Trap: "At least 5 years" and "At least 10 years" are too short to support the multi-year annuity-style payouts and lender risk profile envisaged by reverse mortgage. "At least 30 years" is stricter than the scheme prescribes and would unnecessarily disqualify otherwise eligible borrowers. Note: The 20-year residual-life condition is listed in the NISM Series XVII Retirement Adviser workbook discussion of reverse mortgage eligibility alongside age, ownership, clear title, absence of encumbrance, and primary-residence criteria. The framing above is presented as general scheme-eligibility knowledge drawn from those criteria, not from a specific minimum property-value rule.
